title: Credential dumping on a Windows host
summary: An alert fired for LSASS memory access. Reconstruct how the host was compromised, find the stash, and decide whether to escalate.
briefing: It is 09:15. Your EDR flags an unfamiliar process opening a handle to lsass.exe on a Windows server in the ATTACKRANGE lab. LSASS holds credential material, so this is either a serious incident or a badly behaved admin tool. The host's telemetry has been replayed into Splunk. Work the alert the way a Tier 1 analyst would: orient, triage, hunt, scope, then write a detection and a verdict.

stages.title: Orient
stages.narrative: Before touching the alert, confirm which telemetry actually arrived for this host. Different sensors answer different questions.
stages.question: Which log sources are present for this host?

options: Sysmon, Windows Security, and a CrowdStrike sensor
PowerShell script block logging and a firewall log

checks.spl: index=attack_data host="<HOST>" | stats dc(sourcetype) as sourcetypes values(source) as sources

stages.starter_spl: index=attack_data host="<HOST>" | stats count by sourcetype source | sort -count
hints: Group by sourcetype and source, then look at the source names rather than the event count.
One sensor writes a non-Windows sourcetype.
stages.debrief: Three sources are present: Sysmon (process, file, registry and process-access events), Windows Security (one 4688 process creation) and CrowdStrike sensor data. Sysmon is the richest source here; Security gives an independent process record, and CrowdStrike adds sensor context.

stages.title: Triage the alert
stages.narrative: The alert says lsass.exe was accessed. Normal Windows processes touch LSASS all the time, so identify the process on the other end of the handle.
stages.question: Which tool opened a handle to lsass.exe? (One executable name is enough.)

checks.spl: index=attack_data host="<HOST>" sourcetype=XmlWinEventLog EventCode=10 | search TargetImage="*lsass.exe" | stats values(SourceImage) as tools

stages.starter_spl: index=attack_data host="<HOST>" sourcetype=XmlWinEventLog EventCode=10 | search TargetImage="*lsass.exe" | stats values(SourceImage) as tools values(GrantedAccess) as access
hints: Sysmon event ID 10 is process access. TargetImage is the process being opened; SourceImage is the process doing the opening.
Sort or count by SourceImage to separate normal Windows activity from the noisy outliers.
stages.debrief: Sysmon event 10 shows procdump.exe (and the renamed notprocdump.exe) opening lsass.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1fffff, a full-access mask far beyond normal antivirus or system activity. That mask is the credential-dump signal.

stages.title: Hunt the dump command
stages.narrative: A process access alone does not show intent. Find the command line that tells you what was written, and where.
stages.question: Which file did the tool write the LSASS memory dump to? (File name or full path.)

checks.spl: index=attack_data host="<HOST>" sourcetype=XmlWinEventLog EventCode=1 | search CommandLine="*lsass*" | stats values(CommandLine) as commands

stages.starter_spl: index=attack_data host="<HOST>" sourcetype=XmlWinEventLog EventCode=1 | search CommandLine="*lsass*" | eval Process=coalesce(Image, NewProcessName), Parent=coalesce(ParentImage, ParentProcessName) | table _time Process Parent CommandLine User | sort _time
hints: Process creation is Sysmon event 1 (and Security 4688 for the one record you have). Command lines live there.
Follow the parent chain: PowerShell spawned cmd.exe, which launched the dumper.
stages.debrief: The command line is procdump.exe -accepteula -ma lsass.exe C:\Windows\Temp\lsass_dump.dmp, launched by cmd.exe from PowerShell under ATTACKRANGE\Administrator. The 4688 record independently shows procdump64.exe with the same arguments. The dump was deleted afterwards, which is consistent with anti-forensics, not troubleshooting.

stages.title: Scope the technique
stages.narrative: One dump is an incident; several attempts show a determined actor. Check whether other LSASS-dumping methods were used on this host.
stages.question: Name another tool or technique that also targeted LSASS memory in this dataset.

checks.spl: index=attack_data host="<HOST>" | search CommandLine="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*" OR CommandLine="*sekurlsa*" OR CommandLine="*createdump*" | stats values(CommandLine) as commands

stages.starter_spl: index=attack_data host="<HOST>" | search CommandLine="*lsass*" | eval Process=coalesce(Image, NewProcessName) | stats count values(CommandLine) as commands by EventCode Process | sort -count
hints: Search every command line mentioning lsass, not just procdump.
Look beyond one tool: built-in Windows utilities and credential tooling can also read LSASS memory.
stages.debrief: The host saw several dump attempts: procdump/notprocdump, rundll32 with comsvcs.dll MiniDump, createdump.exe producing dotnet-lsass.dmp, and cmd.exe running mimikatz sekurlsa::minidump. That is a toolkit, not a single tool, and it raises confidence in a true positive.

stages.title: Choose a detection
stages.narrative: You need a detection a defender can keep. Compare the options and pick the one that catches the behavior without drowning the SOC in noise.
stages.question: Which detection would you ship for this behavior?

options: Alert whenever a process named procdump.exe runs
Alert on LSASS access with a full-access mask, or on command lines that dump LSASS memory (procdump, comsvcs MiniDump, mimikatz sekurlsa)
Alert on every Sysmon event ID 10 process-access event

stages.starter_spl: index=attack_data host="<HOST>" sourcetype=XmlWinEventLog | search (EventCode=10 AND TargetImage="*lsass.exe" AND GrantedAccess="0x1fffff") OR CommandLine="*procdump*lsass*" OR CommandLine="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*" | stats count values(CommandLine) as commands by host | where count > 0
hints: A filename-only rule misses renames, and a rule on all process-access events is mostly benign noise.
The strongest signal combines the access mask with the dumping command lines.
stages.debrief: Ship the behavior-based rule. GrantedAccess 0x1fffff on lsass is a full-access read, and the command-line branches cover renames and alternative tooling. A procdump-name rule is trivially evaded by renaming the binary to notprocdump.exe. Alerting on every event 10 buries the analyst in legitimate activity (svchost, taskmgr, security products).

stages.title: Verdict and handoff
stages.narrative: Decide what this is, and write the sentence you would put in the incident ticket. Your explanation is saved for the debrief and is not auto-graded.
stages.question: What is your verdict?

options: True positive: credential dumping. Escalate and treat the account and host as compromised.
False positive: an administrator ran ProcDump for troubleshooting.
Benign: LSASS is accessed by Windows all the time, so close the alert.

stages.starter_spl: index=attack_data host="<HOST>" sourcetype=XmlWinEventLog (EventCode=1 OR EventCode=4688) | eval Process=coalesce(Image, NewProcessName), Parent=coalesce(ParentImage, ParentProcessName), Account=coalesce(User, SubjectUserName) | table _time EventCode Process Parent CommandLine Account | sort _time | head 100
hints: Weigh who ran it, from which parent process, with what access mask, and what happened to the dump file afterwards.
A legitimate admin dump would be explained by a ticket or change record, not launched from a PowerShell chain and then deleted.
stages.debrief: This is a true positive. Evidence: full-access LSASS access by procdump/notprocdump, an explicit dump path under C:\Windows\Temp, a parent chain from PowerShell through cmd.exe, and several alternative dump techniques on the same host. Escalate, reset the account's credentials, and hunt for use of the stolen material elsewhere.

debrief: Verdict: true positive credential dumping (T1003.001) on host cc9b25d6-efc9-11eb-926b-550bf0943fbb. Evidence: Sysmon event 10 shows procdump.exe and notprocdump.exe opening lsass.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1fffff; Sysmon event 1 and Security 4688 show procdump.exe -ma lsass.exe C:\Windows\Temp\lsass_dump.dmp spawned from PowerShell/cmd.exe under ATTACKRANGE\Administrator; the same host also used rundll32 + comsvcs.dll MiniDump, createdump.exe and mimikatz sekurlsa. The dump was deleted after use. Respond by isolating the host, resetting the account, and searching for the dumped credentials in later authentication. Tuning note: baseline legitimate LSASS access (security products, backup agents) and alert on full-access masks plus dumping command lines rather than on process names.
